ap-scores-delayed-missing-2026.heading: Three missing-score cases
ap-scores-delayed-missing-2026.intro: Fictional examples using the 2026 release. Start by checking your own College Board score report, then verify any college requirement directly.

examples.title: One result is missing from your account
examples.question: It is November 2026. You see AP English Language in your original College Board account, but AP Chemistry from a late-testing date is still absent. What would you do first?
steps: Write down the subject, late-testing date and school. Note that another 2026 score appears in the same account.
The August 15 support checkpoint has passed. Contact AP Services for Students with those facts. Ask whether it can locate the Chemistry exam record.
examples.mistake: Late testing might explain an initial delay, but it does not identify what is holding this specific score now.
examples.check: What if you cannot sign in to the account you used for AP?
examples.answer: Use College Board's account recovery help first. Creating another account can complicate matching.

examples.title: Your college has not posted a visible score
examples.question: Your AP Biology score appears in College Board. Your order history shows the report was made available to the correct college, but its student portal has not posted the credit. Would another report address the problem?
steps: Check that the reporting recipient matches the college you attend and that the report includes the Biology result.
Ask the college's registrar or admissions office whether it matched the report and when its placement or credit decision is due.
examples.mistake: Available to the recipient does not mean processed by the college. Paying for another report would not confirm that processing occurred.
examples.check: What if your order history shows a different college?
examples.answer: Confirm the correct recipient and the required report with your college. A report sent to one college is not delivery to another.

examples.title: Placement is due while a score is still pending
examples.question: Your college already received a 2026 AP report with the available results, but you need the missing Calculus result for placement. Registration opens next week. Can you count on an automatic update in time?
steps: Check that the college was designated to receive your scores from that exam year. College Board can send a delayed score automatically once it becomes available.
Contact AP Services about the absent 2026 result and ask the college how to register while placement is pending. Keep the two conversations separate.
examples.mistake: Automatic sending has no guaranteed date for the score to appear or the college to apply it. Ordering another report does not create the absent score.
examples.check: What if the college confirms it accepts an alternative placement test?
examples.answer: Check its deadline and how the result would affect registration. Follow the confirmed option while you resolve the AP record with AP Services.

sat-score-release-guide.heading: Three application deadlines, three different decisions
sat-score-release-guide.intro: College Board lists December 18, 2026 as the student release date for the December 5 SAT Weekend. The college rules and deadlines below are fictional. Use your own college's written policy and verify when your score actually appears.

examples.title: A college accepts self-reporting
examples.question: Your college accepts the December SAT and lets you enter scores in its application portal through December 20. Your score appears December 18. Do you need to order an official score report to meet this deadline?
steps: Use the college's self-reporting field and confirm the portal shows the score was submitted before its cutoff.
Save the submission confirmation. Check when the college requires an official report, if it does; it might be needed later rather than with the application.
examples.mistake: Avoid paying for delivery just because the application deadline is close. A self-reporting deadline is not the same as an official receipt deadline.
examples.check: What if the college does not accept self-reported scores?
examples.answer: Follow the college's official receipt rule. Entering your score in a text box is not a substitute for a required official report.

examples.title: A college must receive the official report
examples.question: Your score appears Friday, December 18. The college accepts the December test but requires the official report by Monday, December 21. Would ordering on Friday give you a reliable delivery plan?
steps: Standard delivery is typically sent 5 to 10 business days after you order; the weekend does not leave that much time.

Rush is available only after release and is sent in 1 to 4 business days, excluding weekends and holidays. Even the fastest end of that range leaves no time to spare. The college may need more time to match the report to your application.
Before paying, ask whether the college can use an earlier score, accept a pending score, or honor a separate materials deadline. If it cannot, plan using the written requirement.
examples.mistake: An order receipt is not a delivery confirmation, and a report marked sent is not necessarily posted to your application.
examples.check: What if the portal shows a different materials deadline from the application deadline?
examples.answer: Verify which cutoff applies to official scores, which test dates the college accepts, and what the deadline means: ordered, received, or matched. Use the college's confirmed rule.

examples.title: The deadline comes before the scheduled release
examples.question: Your college needs scores by December 15. Your new December SAT score is scheduled for December 18, and you already have a score from an earlier test. Can a rush order make the December score usable by December 15?
steps: No. Rush applies to released scores only. The new score is not scheduled to be available by the college's deadline.
Check whether the earlier sitting is accepted and how to report it. Ask about a later materials cutoff only if the college's policy leaves that unclear.
examples.mistake: An SAT date before the application deadline is not enough. Compare the accepted test date and the score deadline separately.
examples.check: What if the college is test optional for your program?
examples.answer: Check whether the program, scholarship or applicant category has an exception. If the college confirms you can apply without a score, that is a separate option from ordering an older report.

sat-math-score-guide.heading: Work an error through to a new problem
sat-math-score-guide.intro: Original teaching examples, not College Board questions or a score estimate. Try each problem before opening the reasoning, then test the same skill with the changed problem.

examples.title: Find the first wrong step
examples.question: A student changes 4(2x - 3) = 20 into 8x - 3 = 20 and obtains x = 23/8. Identify the first error, then solve and check the original equation.
steps: The factor 4 multiplies both terms inside the parentheses: 8x - 12 = 20, not 8x - 3 = 20.
Add 12 to both sides: 8x = 32. Divide by 8: x = 4.
Substitute into the original equation: 4(2 times 4 - 3) = 4 times 5 = 20. The answer satisfies the original, not just a later line.
examples.mistake: Review label: distribution. If you reached 23/8, the issue was the first expansion, not division at the end. On your next practice problem, write the expanded line explicitly.
examples.check: Changed problem: solve 3(2x - 5) = 21. Write the expanded line and one substitution check before opening the answer.
examples.answer: 6x - 15 = 21; 6x = 36; x = 6. Check: 3(2 times 6 - 5) = 3 times 7 = 21. Both terms were multiplied by 3.

examples.title: Separate a starting amount from a rate
examples.question: A bicycle rental costs a fixed $8 plus $3 per hour. A student writes C = 8h + 3. What is wrong with the model, and what should a two-hour rental cost?
steps: Let h be rental time in hours and C be cost in dollars. Each additional hour adds $3, so the variable part is 3h.
The fixed $8 does not depend on hours. Add it once: C = 3h + 8.
For two hours, C = 3(2) + 8 = $14. The student's model gives $19 because it incorrectly makes $8 the hourly rate.
Check the structure: when h increases by 1, the correct model increases C by $3. The units of 3h are dollars per hour times hours, which is dollars.
examples.mistake: Review label: interpreting a linear model. A calculator can evaluate either model, but cannot decide which quantity is the rate. Label the rate and fixed amount before calculating.
examples.check: Changed problem: another rental uses C = 5h + 12. Interpret 12, then calculate the total for three hours and the additional cost of one more hour.
examples.answer: 12 is the fixed starting cost, in dollars. Three hours cost 5(3) + 12 = $27. One additional hour adds $5, not another $12.

sat-reading-writing-score-guide.heading: Test the reason behind an answer
sat-reading-writing-score-guide.intro: Original teaching examples, not College Board questions or a score estimate. Choose an answer before opening the reasoning. The changed question checks whether the reason transfers beyond a memorized answer.

examples.title: Choose the relationship, not a familiar phrase
examples.question: A library predicted that longer evening hours would increase attendance. It stayed open two hours later for a month. ___, its evening attendance remained unchanged. Which transition fits: A. Consequently; B. However; C. For example; D. Similarly?
steps: Compare the prediction with the outcome. The library expected an increase, but attendance stayed the same. The relationship is contrast.
B, However, marks that contrast. A, Consequently, would emphasize an effect rather than the failure of the stated prediction.
C, For example, would require a general statement that this outcome illustrates. D, Similarly, would require a comparable result already described. Neither relationship is supplied.
examples.mistake: Review label: transitions. All four choices can begin a sentence grammatically. Grammar alone cannot choose between them; first state the relationship between the ideas in your own words.
examples.check: Changed question: a library wanted to make its services easier to access. ___, it extended evening hours and added a weekend book-return point. Which choice fits: For example, However, or Nevertheless? Explain what the second sentence does.
examples.answer: For example. Extending hours and adding a return point illustrate the general aim of easier access. However and Nevertheless would signal an opposition that this text does not establish.

examples.title: Match a conclusion to the evidence's scope
examples.question: In one class, the average practice score rose from 61 to 65 after a new study routine was introduced. There was no comparison class. Which conclusion is supported: A. Every student improved; B. The routine caused the increase; C. This class's average was four points higher afterward; D. The routine works better for all students?
steps: The two reported averages establish a four-point increase for this class. C stays within those observations.
A is too broad: an average does not show each student's change. For example, scores of 50 and 72 average 61; scores of 48 and 82 average 65 even though one score fell.

B adds causation that a before-and-after observation without a comparison does not establish. D extends one class to all students and adds a comparison with other methods. Neither claim is given by the evidence.
examples.mistake: Review label: evidence and inference. A choice may repeat the right topic while adding every, caused, or all. Check the population, comparison and strength of the claim against the actual observations.
examples.check: Changed question: both classes improved, but the report gives only their averages and no individual results. Can you conclude that every student in either class improved? What narrower statement could you make?
examples.answer: No. You can report that each class's average increased, but not that every individual's score rose. The numerical counterexample above shows why those are different claims.
